source.title: Challenging the N-Heuristic: Effect size, not sample size, predicts the replicability of psychological science
source.coverage: Retained prior coverage: Introduction PDF page 3, Method pages 4–5, Results pages 6–8, Discussion pages 12–13. Fresh resumed conversation reread the original readable source, with focused inspection of Results pages 6–8 and Introduction page 3. Full-paper reading not claimed; supporting-information files and OSF data/code were not retrieved or reanalyzed. Studies and survey respondents are nonrepresentative.

position.target: Distinguish separate and joint predictor models, and explain why diagnostic associations do not show N is causally irrelevant
position.location: Fresh resumed conversation stopped after one reasoning check on the joint model’s conditional diagnostic association versus an intervention claim (Results PDF pages 6–8; Introduction page 3). The check was unanswered. Researcher inputs were scripted by an evaluator, not evidence of actual human learning.

explained: Original-study N covers the original conditions later retested, not replication-study sample size.
Separate study-design-controlled models: log N B=0.20, p=0.214; log effect size B=0.64, p=0.006.
Joint model: N B=0.56, p=0.005; effect size B=1.03, p=0.0002. Positive conditional associations and N/effect-size r_s=-0.49 are consistent with suppression, not causal identification.
Nonsignificance does not establish no role; significance does not establish causation. Authors retain all-else-equal benefit of larger N for power.
A runner/load analogy was explicitly supplementary explanation, not paper evidence.

understanding.point: Across-study comparison differs from increasing N within the same study
understanding.answer: The model compares different studies, so it is not a same-study increase in N.
understanding.reason: The scripted answer accurately identifies the unit of comparison. Credit is restricted to this distinction, not the causal conclusion or the chapter.

understanding.answer: But since N was not significant and effect size was, the paper proves that a large effect causes replication and sample size never matters.
understanding.reason: The same answer recognized the across-study comparison but incorrectly inferred effect-size causation and universal N irrelevance. Correction was explained; no subsequent answer demonstrated the repaired inference.

understanding.point: Why the separate and joint models give different N results
understanding.answer: I do not know how N can be nonsignificant in one model but significant in the joint model. Please help me.
understanding.reason: Suppression and conditional association were explained. The smaller check was unanswered; direct explanation and stopping do not establish understanding.

gaps: An answer-supported explanation of the joint model's conditional association and the pattern consistent with suppression.
An answer-supported correction of claims that effect size causes replication or N never matters.
No chapter-level mastery established; no empirical reanalysis or generalization beyond the source scope.
next_entry: If this target is resumed, reread Results pages 6–8 and Introduction page 3, and return to the unanswered check: rewrite the claim that the joint model proves increasing N causes any study to replicate as a conditional diagnostic association. Respect the researcher’s requested mode; no new verification occurred during resuming or stopping.
